conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in last night because of trouble breathing. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I couldn’t catch my breath. Yesterday I couldn’t walk a block without stopping. This morning, I was gasping in bed. Sitting up helped a little, but then I got worse going to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chest pain, fever, or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chest pain. Just some belly discomfort last night. No fever or throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We know you have heart and lung issues, including from past crack use. We started you on oxygen and some meds in the ER to help your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t smoked crack lately. I’ve been going to that rehab program. Just cigarettes now and then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We checked your heart with an ultrasound, and your ejection fraction is down to 20%. That means your heart isn’t pumping as well as it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that worse than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s lower than your last admission. We’ve increased your carvedilol and given IV furosemide to remove fluid. Your lungs are clearing up already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my heart again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. But your chest X-ray also shows lung irritation — likely from past crack use, not infection. Pulmonary team thinks it’s hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your labs don’t show infection, so we stopped antibiotics after one dose. We’re treating you with steroids to calm the lung inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? Like prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll be on a 20-day taper — starting high and slowly decreasing. It should help your breathing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on those before. They make my blood sugar go crazy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your glucose was 316 when you arrived. We’ve increased your Lantus to 60 units twice daily and are using a sliding scale. We’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I don’t want to get into DKA again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your sugars regularly. You haven’t ketones, so that’s good. Your breathing is already better than in the ER, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, much better. I can breathe sitting up now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re moving you to the regular floor today. Your lungs are clearer, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your repeat X-ray shows mild improvement. The lung opacities are still there, but you’re doing well on room air now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The steroids are helping. We’ll keep you on oral lasix 40mg daily. No more IV. You’re euvolemic — not retaining fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heart? Is it going to get stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve optimized your meds. You’re on carvedilol 12.5mg twice daily now. You have a cardiology follow-up to discuss an AICD for protection against sudden cardiac death.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With an EF of 20%, it’s strongly recommended. Your heart is weak, and an AICD can prevent sudden rhythm problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll go to the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars are still high — up to 400 — but no ketones. We’re keeping your insulin aggressive. As the steroids taper, we’ll adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. I’m eating right, but the steroids are wrecking my levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re discharging you on 60 units Lantus twice daily and a sliding scale. You’ll need to check your sugars four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a glucometer at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you one, plus test strips. And you’re continuing with your dual diagnosis program?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m committed. I don’t want to keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your schizophrenia is stable on quetiapine. No signs of psychosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Off oxygen, walking the hall, saturating in the 90s on room air. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds am I taking at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, but carvedilol is now 12.5mg twice daily, and you’re on a prednisone taper: 60mg daily for 2 days, then down over 17 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lantus 60 units at breakfast and bedtime. Novolog with meals based on your sliding scale. Watch for highs as the steroids go down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the rehab program?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should return to your dual diagnosis program. They’ll support your recovery. You also have outpatient rehab for physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lung tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hypersensitivity panel is still pending. You have a follow-up with pulmonary for PFTs and more testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re breathing well, sugars are manageable, and your heart is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going home with my sister?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weigh yourself every morning. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds. And if you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or sugar over 400, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work with your program. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Breathing easy. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lungs are clear, heart rate normal. You’re doing great. Remember your steroid taper, sugar checks, and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it day by day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best way. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your meds and supplies now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.
